This would have to be done in conjunction with existing State requirements for shaping and grading, but should present no insurmountable problems.
Some areas of the raw spoils to be produced by mining on the tracts are expected to be too saline or alkaline for most crop species (Colorado School of Mines Research Institute, 1975). These areas have been generally located, but additional testing of overburden would be required as mining and reclamation progress. If problem areas can be given special treatment to isolate toxic overburden (via selective placement at depth in the reconstructed landform), or if adequate depths of suitable topsoil and subsoil materials can be provided, it might be possible to farm much of the reclaimed lands.
Further study must be done to compare the costs and benefits (over the long term) of reclaiming the land to support various types and degrees of farming. For example, very little additional treatment of problem spoils might be needed to allow production of crops such as barley which are very tolerant of saline and alkaline conditions. While this would be a cheaper form of reclamation for the mining company, it might severely limit future options for use of the land, especially for agriculture. More expensive (in the short term) reclamation techniques, including adequate topsoiling and/or selective materials placement during mining, might be economically justified over the long term if these treatments allowed production of more diverse and valuable crops on the land.
